newsitem.title: USA: No new U.S. aid seen until N. Korea replies on talks.
newsitem.headline: No new U.S. aid seen until N. Korea replies on talks.

text.p: Despite Pyongyang's demands, no new U.S. food aid pledges are expected before North Korea responds conclusively to a proposal for Korean peninsula peace talks, U.S. officials said on Thursday.

They told Reuters North Korea began Wednesday's crucial meeting in New York by essentially accepting a U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks but then tied that acceptance to a new demand for international assistance to meet severe food shortages.

As a result, "we don't have a deal," one official said, although the U.S. presumption remains that Pyongyang will respond positively to the proposal when talks involving negotiators for the United States, North Korea and arch-rival South Korea resume in New York on Friday.

Another official said the United States worked hard to avoid being put in a position where food aid was seen as a reward for North Korea's acceptance of the peace talks proposal. Washington sped normal bureaucratic procedures to announce an extra $15 million in assistance last Monday.
Asked if he expected the United States or South Korea to announce additional food aid before talks resume on Friday, the official said: "No, I don't."

"My expectation is that sooner or later the North Koreans are going to feel they accomplished their first priority: They sensitized the outside world to their needs ... and they will turn to the question of peace talks and give a response. I'm still expecting that response will be favourable," he said.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns confirmed that Washington planned no new food aid commitments at this time. "I think the United States has done what it can. I'm not aware of any initiative within the State Department or the U.S. government to see if we would ratchet that up," he said.
Acting Assistant Secretary of State Charles Kartman, head of the U.S. delegation negotiating with Pyongyang, reported "encouraging progress" when talks adjourned on Wednesday.
When they resume on Friday, Burns said, "we hope that at the end of the day we'll be able to say North Korea agrees to four-party talks."

The meeting was called to hear Pyongyang's formal response to a year-old U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks, in which China would also participate, that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing the fraying armistice with a peace treaty.
After some scepticism in Washington and elsewhere, it has been widely accepted that impoverished Stalinist North Korea is facing serious food shortages bordering on famine.

North Korea and independent experts say the country needs 2.3 million tons of food this year. Pyongyang claims it can scrape together about half that amount, with the rest coming from international donors. Some U.S. analysts doubt this.

The U.N. World Food Programme recently appealed for 200,000 metric tons of food, with Washington offering one-quarter. An official who spoke anonymously said U.S. negotiators have tried to explain to the North Koreans that "there isn't a disagreement about their need" and Washington was dealing with that in the appropriate place, the World Food Programme.

He said the problem was that North Korea keeps "talking about their total need and their desire to have Santa Claus say that it's all going to be taken care of. And that isn't the way it's going to work," the official said.
Humanitarian activists on Thursday pressed Japan to donate some of its rice hoard to North Korea and urged the United States to work with China to speed delivery of food aid.
Representative Tony Hall, who visited North Korea this month, said Japan has about 250,000-350,000 tons of old rice that has little potential for domestic consumption.

With famine projected to begin in late May or early June in North Korea, Andrew Natsios of the charity World Vision U.S. suggested a food swap in which China would provide 50,000 tons of corn now and accept a promised 50,000-ton U.S. aid shipment, which will take several months to arrive, to replenish its supplies.

Officials at the U.S. Agency for International Development, which handles donations to North Korea, said sizable quantities of food would arrive in North Korea in the next few weeks so a swap with China did not appear necessary.
